item.title: “One who once was heedless and later is not, Illumines the world like the moon freed from clouds.” “He who deeds of merit makes, And…
item.description:
“One who once was heedless and later is not,
Illumines the world like the moon freed from clouds.”

“He who deeds of merit makes,
And thereby his evil deeds dispels,
Illumines the world like the moon freed from clouds.”

“Blinded is this world,
Few are those who see clearly.
Like birds escaped from a net,
Few go to heaven.”

“Like a swan flying through the sky,
With psychic power soaring through space,
Having conquered Māra and his host,
The wise one leaves this world behind.”

From: Dhammapada 167-178

item.title: “He contemplates all forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as…
item.description:
“He contemplates all forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. He turns his mind away from these states and directs it towards the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime—namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ If he is firm in this, he attains the destruction of the defilements. If he does not yet attain the destruction of the defilements, then by that same Dhamma-lust, Dhamma-delight, and by the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is reborn spontaneously (in the Pure Abodes) and there attains final Nibbāna, never to return from that world.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 64 – Mahāmāluṅkyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And Nigrodha, there are unwholesome states that have not been abandoned, that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, bringing suffering, resulting in pain, leading to…
item.description:
“And Nigrodha, there are unwholesome states that have not been abandoned, that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, bringing suffering, resulting in pain, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Those states I teach for the purpose of abandoning them. If you practice in accordance with the teaching, then those defiling states will be abandoned, the pure states will increase, and you will personally know, realize, and attain to abiding here and now with perfect and complete wisdom.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 25 – Udumbarikasutta

item.title: “O good friends, here someone associates with sensual pleasures, associates with unwholesome states. After some time, that person hears the noble Dhamma, gives wise attention,…
item.description:
“O good friends, here someone associates with sensual pleasures, associates with unwholesome states. After some time, that person hears the noble Dhamma, gives wise attention, and attains the true Dhamma and the Dhamma in accordance. And having heard the noble Dhamma, given wise attention, and attained the true Dhamma and the Dhamma in accordance, that person lives without associating with sensual pleasures, without associating with unwholesome states. By living without associating with sensual pleasures, without associating with unwholesome states, ease arises, and more than ease, gladness arises. O good friends, just as from comfort joy is born, so too, O good friends, by living without associating with sensual pleasures, without associating with unwholesome states, ease arises, and more than ease, gladness arises. O good friends, that is the first short path leading to ease, realized by the Blessed One, the Wise One, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

From: Dīgha Nikāya 18 – Janavasabhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island,…
item.description:
“Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body internally, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world. Thus, monks, a monk lives as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 26 – Cakkavattisutta

item.title: “Cunda, just as all unwholesome states tend downward and all wholesome states tend upward. So too, Cunda: the harmless person is higher than the harmful…
item.description:
“Cunda, just as all unwholesome states tend downward and all wholesome states tend upward. So too, Cunda: the harmless person is higher than the harmful person; the person who abstains from killing is higher than the killer; the person who abstains from taking what is not given is higher than the taker of what is not given; the person unsmeared by the world, not clinging to personal views, of easy disposition and equanimity, is higher than the person smeared by the world, clinging to personal views, of difficult disposition and lacking equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 8 – Sallekhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Again, the five kinds of kings Are present in the world — Learn to subdue them, Always keeping mindfulness. Toward forms and sounds, Toward tastes…
item.description:
“Again, the five kinds of kings
Are present in the world —
Learn to subdue them,
Always keeping mindfulness.
Toward forms and sounds,
Toward tastes and smells,
And toward contacts —
Subdue desire and lust.

Subdue desire
For these things.
The mindful monk,
With mind well liberated,
Then, at the right time,
Rightly reflecting on the Dhamma,
With unified mind,
He should destroy darkness.” So spoke the Blessed One.

From: Sutta Nipāta 4.16
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - What oppresses the world? What envelops the world? What arrow pierces the world? With what is it always smeared? - Death oppresses the world,…
item.description:
- What oppresses the world?
What envelops the world?
What arrow pierces the world?
With what is it always smeared?
- Death oppresses the world,
Aging envelops the world,
The arrow of craving pierces the world,
With sensual desires it is always smeared.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.66

item.title: “Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms,…
item.description:
“Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then, monks, this is called a monk who has gone into Māra’s domain, who has come under Māra’s control. Māra’s net has surrounded him. Bound by Māra, he is subject to the Evil One’s will. Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye … If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, monks, this is called a monk who has not gone into Māra’s domain, not come under Māra’s control. Māra’s net has not surrounded him. Freed from Māra’s bondage, he is not subject to the Evil One’s will.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.114
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, for a monk, those defilements that should be abandoned by direct knowledge have been abandoned by direct knowledge; those defilements that should be abandoned…
item.description:
“Monks, for a monk, those defilements that should be abandoned by direct knowledge have been abandoned by direct knowledge; those defilements that should be abandoned by restraint have been abandoned by restraint … That monk is called one who lives restrained by the restraint of all defilements, who has cut off craving, has shed the fetters, has rightly penetrated conceit, and has made an end of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 2 – Sabbāsavasutta
